paragraphs.text: Half of this lesson is already in your notebook; this page is about getting it out again on demand. A word you met once in a list waits passively. A word you filed inside a map — with a place on the branch and a neighbour on the same twig — is a word you can walk to.

The example map starts from one centre, {{de:Essen und Trinken}}, and splits it four ways, so each branch answers a different question about the same topic: what is on the plate, what is in the glass, where you buy it, and when you eat it.
Essen und Trinken → Lebensmittel (das Brot) · Getränke (das Wasser) · Geschäfte (die Bäckerei) · Mahlzeiten (das Frühstück)

The second method is pairs: words that keep each other company in real speech. Salt calls for pepper, vinegar for oil, bread for rolls. Say the pair, not the item — you then retrieve two words for the price of one, and the second word arrives before you have to search for it.

The third is free association: put a word in the middle and write whatever it triggers, without judging the result. Groups will disagree about what belongs together, and that argument is itself useful — you remember the words you had to defend.

blocks.prompt: Complete each pair — which word keeps this one company?

items.hint: what you buy at the market
